Concern over delay in implementation of Delhi Land Pooling Policy and finalization of Master Plan Delhi-2041.
details:
Shri Neeraj Dangi: 
The prolonged delay in implementing Delhi Land
Pooling Policy (LPP) and finalizing the Master Plan for Delhi-2041, both of
which are critical to planned urban development in the National Capital. Land
Pooling Policy was notified in 2013 as a transformative reform intended to
enable participatory, planned urban expansion through voluntary land pooling by
landowners. Subsequent modifications introduced in 2018, including reduction of
Floor Area Ratio from 400 to 200 and mandatory consortium formation
requirement, have created practical difficulties for small and individual
landowners. As a result, even after a decade, policy remains largely
unimplemented. This prolonged uncertainty has caused severe hardship to
farmers, villagers, and middle-class investors who had placed their faith in
the promise of affordable housing and planned development. Many landowners
invested their life savings through cooperative and welfare societies,
expecting that the policy would unlock development opportunities. Instead,
their lands remain locked, infrastructure development stalled, and frustration
has led to increase in litigation. Situation further aggravated by delay in
finalizing Master Plan Delhi-2041, which is essential for enabling sector
planning and infrastructure rollout. In absence of this overarching planning
framework, implementation of Land Pooling Policy has effectively come to a
standstill. I therefore urge the Government to consider mission-mode
implementation of the Land Pooling Policy with clear and time-bound roadmap,
rationalise procedural bottlenecks affecting small landowners, establish an
appropriate institutional mechanism for coordinated execution, and expedite
final notification of Master Plan Delhi-2041 so that planned development,
investor confidence, and aspirations of lakhs of landowners can be restored.
(ENDS)

Directions regarding mandatory displaying the Preamble of Constitution of India in to all the Government institutions.
details:
Shri
Neeraj Dangi: The Government of India has mandated the display of Mahatma
Gandhis portrait in all government offices, public institutions and courts, as
a mark of respect and to inspire citizens. All government institutions have
been directed to display Dr. Ambedkars portrait also, recognizing his
contributions to social justice, equality, and the Constitution of India. This
mandate is based on Supreme Court directives and various Government
notifications & circulars from 2013 to 2019.? Compulsory displaying these
portraits serves as a reminder of their contributions to Indias freedom,
social justice, and constitutional values. In year 2019, the Supreme Court
directed all educational institutions to display the Preamble Constitution of
India in their premises. Displaying the Preamble acknowledges it?s significance
as an integral part of the Constitution and Indias governance framework. Like
all schools and educational institutions, all government institutions should
also display the Preamble prominently, fostering a sense of national unity,
values, and constitutional responsibility. The display of Preamble of The
Constitution of India in all government institution will: firstly,??? Promote
national integration, reflecting the countrys commitment to sovereignty,
socialism, secularism, and democracy; secondly, Embodies the fundamental values and
principles enshrined in the Constitution, serving as a reminder to public servants; thirdly, Inspire
and educate citizens, about Indias constitutional heritage and core values ;
fourthly, Symbolize the national pride and identity, reflecting the countrys
history, philosophy and aspirations. Therefore I, urge Government of India to
issue appropriate direction to all Government institutions for mandatory
displaying the Preamble of the Constitution of India in their premises.
(Ends)

Demand to amend the Companies Rules for representation of SC, ST and OBC on the Board of Directors.
details:
SHRI NEERAJ
DANGI (Rajasthan): Thank
you Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, for allowing me to raise this important issue in
the House. As per Rule 3 of Companies (Appointment and Qualification of
Directors) Rules, 2014, every listed company or any other public company,
having certain paid-up share capital or turnover shall appoint, at least, one
woman Director. This step was taken by the Government to have a fair
representation of women in the Corporate Board Room, who constitute around 50
per cent of population.
Why cant a
similar provision be made for SC-ST-OBCs who constitute around 85 per cent of
the countrys population and have negligible representation in the Board of
Directors?
The SC-ST-OBCs
communities rarely enter into board room even though they are meritorious and
qualified enough. This has not only demoralised them but most of them have also
lost confidence in top management. 
Recently, the
Parliamentary Standing Committee has expressed its displeasure that there is no
SC or ST member in the Board of Directors of most of the PSUs to adequately
safeguard their interests.
Therefore, Mr.
Deputy Chairman, Sir, through you, I would like to request the Government of
India to amend the companies rules for representation of SC-ST-OBC in the Board
of Directors.
(Ends)

records.title: Concern over unregulated fee hike by IIMs.
details:
SHRI
NEERAJ DANGI (Rajasthan): Sir, unregulated fee hike by IIMs is a matter of
serious concern. The concept of IIM was initiated by Pandit
Jawaharlal Nehru, on the recommendation of Planning Commission in 1960, with
the aim to produce human capital with managerial and decision-making skills
needed to promote industrialisation in the country.
IIM Act, 2017 tenders autonomy to IIMs for fee regulations and student intake.
The autonomy plays a significant role in incentivising
the IIMs. The fee hike for the academic year 2020-2022, the average fee in old
IIMs is Rs.20.7 lakh; those in new IIMs is Rs.13.7 lakh, for two-year full time course. On the other hand, the
management institutions under UGC and AICTE are restricted by the AICTE
notification dated May 1, 2020 for fee hike. The lack of accountability owing
to an absence of Government intervention leads to more questions than answers.
Fee hike in IIM inches the hump of a hurdle for eligible aspirants particularly
from middle class and deprived to acquire managerial skills. The present
scenario compromises a very fundamental objective of education in the country
that aims to provide accessibility and affordability to the prospective and
existing workforce.? Fee hike in premier
management institutions leaves middle-class eligible aspirants with the only
option of education loan to fund their dreams. Increasing
fees of IIMs balloons loan requirement significantly. This fee hike will
thwart aspirants dreams of acquiring managerial skills. I urge the Government
of India to critically observe and amend the fee structure of IIMs. 
(Ends)
